claim: The crystal structure of HUWE1 (3951-4374) was determined at 2.7 Å resolution by molecular replacement using PDB ID: 3H1D as a search model.
source: We determined the crystal structure of this construct at 2.7 Å resolution by molecular replacement, using a structure of the HUWE1 HECT domain (PDB ID: 3H1D [Pandya et al., 2010]) as a search model.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the resolution and method used for structure determination, with reference to the search model.

claim: The crystal structure of HUWE1 (3951-4374) has two molecules in the asymmetric unit.
source: The structure has two molecules of HUWE1 in the asymmetric unit.
evidence: Directly stated in the text describing the crystal structure.

claim: The HECT domain adopts an overall similar structure in both molecules with a backbone-RMSD of approximately 0.5 Å.
source: The HECT domain adopts an overall similar structure in both molecules (backbone-RMSD ~0.5 Å), in which the HECT C-lobe occupies a centric position along the N-lobe (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative structural comparison data and references Figure 1A,B.

claim: The HECT C-lobe occupies a centric position along the N-lobe in a 'T'-shape conformation.
source: The HECT domain adopts an overall similar structure in both molecules (backbone-RMSD ~0.5 Å), in which the HECT C-lobe occupies a centric position along the N-lobe (Figure 1A,B). Such a conformation has been referred to as 'T'-shape (Verdecia et al., 2003; Lorenz et al., 2013) and is also seen in structures of the isolated HECT domain of HUWE1 (PDB IDs: 3H1D [Pandya et al., 2010] and 3G1N).
evidence: The text describes the conformation and cites previous literature that defined this conformation type.

claim: The conformation of the N-terminal extension differs between the two molecules in the asymmetric unit.
source: However, the conformation of the N-terminal extension differs between the two molecules in the asymmetric unit (Figure 1B).
evidence: Explicitly stated with reference to Figure 1B showing the structural difference.

claim: In molecule A, residues 3979-3990 fold into an α-helix termed the 'thumb helix'.
source: In molecule A, the C-terminal part of the extension (residues 3979–3990) that directly flanks the HECT domain, folds into an α-helix that we will refer to as the 'thumb helix'.
evidence: The text explicitly describes the secondary structure and nomenclature for this region.

claim: In molecule B, the same region (corresponding to the thumb helix in molecule A) adopts a turn followed by short 310-helical segments.
source: In contrast, the same region adopts a turn followed by short 310-helical segments in molecule B.
evidence: Directly stated as a contrast to the structure in molecule A.

claim: The N-terminal part of the extension consists of a long amphipathic α-helix spanning 21 residues (3951-3971) in molecule A and 22 residues (3951-3972) in molecule B, termed the 'pointer helix'.
source: The N-terminal part of the extension consists of a long amphipathic α-helix spanning 21 (3951–3971) and 22 (3951–3972) residues in molecules A and B, respectively, that we will term the 'pointer helix'.
evidence: The text provides specific residue ranges and nomenclature for this structural element.

claim: The pointer helix of molecule A points away from the HECT domain and contacts molecule B.
source: Interestingly, the pointer helix of molecule A points away from the HECT domain and contacts molecule B, where its hydrophobic helix face is grasped tightly by the thumb, the pointer helix, and part of the C-lobe of molecule B (Figure 1C).
evidence: The text describes the structural arrangement with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: The asymmetric dimer interface buries a solvent-accessible surface area of approximately 1350 Å² of molecule A and approximately 1340 Å² of molecule B.
source: The resulting asymmetric dimer interface buries a solvent-accessible surface area of ~1350 Å2 of molecule A and ~1340 Å2 of molecule B.
evidence: Quantitative measurement of the dimer interface is explicitly stated.

claim: The PISA interface scoring program predicts a significant solvation free-energy gain upon dimer formation of −26 kcal/mol.
source: Interface scoring programs, such as the 'Protein interfaces, surfaces and assemblies' service PISA at the European Bioinformatics Institute (http://www.ebi.ac.uk/pdbe/prot_int/pistart.html) (Krissinel and Henrick, 2007) predict a significant solvation free-energy gain upon dimer formation of −26 kcal/mol, indicating that the underlying contacts are extraordinarily hydrophobic.
evidence: The text cites computational prediction results from PISA analysis.

claim: The dimer interface contacts are extraordinarily hydrophobic.
source: Interface scoring programs, such as the 'Protein interfaces, surfaces and assemblies' service PISA at the European Bioinformatics Institute (http://www.ebi.ac.uk/pdbe/prot_int/pistart.html) (Krissinel and Henrick, 2007) predict a significant solvation free-energy gain upon dimer formation of −26 kcal/mol, indicating that the underlying contacts are extraordinarily hydrophobic.
evidence: The inference is drawn from the PISA prediction results.

claim: The extensive hydrophobic contact network at the dimer interface includes residues Phe 3955, Phe 3958, Ala 3959, His 3962, Val 3965, Leu 3966, Ile 3969, Val 3984, Leu 3985, Tyr 3988, and Val 3991.
source: As illustrated by an open-book view of the dimer interface and a contact schematic (Figure 2A,B), the extensive hydrophobic contact network stretches all along the thumb and pointer helices of both molecules and includes Phe 3955, Phe 3958, Ala 3959, His 3962, Val 3965, Leu 3966, Ile 3969, Val 3984, Leu 3985, Tyr 3988, and Val 3991.
evidence: The text lists specific residues involved in the interface with reference to Figure 2A,B.

claim: The thumb region of molecule B is tilted outwards with respect to the HECT domain, allowing it to cradle the C-terminal part of the pointer helix of molecule A.
source: For instance, the thumb region of molecule B, which is re-organized structurally compared to molecule A, is tilted outwards with respect to the HECT domain, thus allowing it to cradle the C-terminal part of the pointer helix of molecule A (Figure 1C).
evidence: The text describes the structural arrangement with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Phe 3982 of molecule B occupies a central position at the dimer interface.
source: This configuration brings Phe 3982 of molecule B into a central position at the interface (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: The text explicitly states the position of this residue with reference to figures.

claim: The C-lobe of molecule B is conformationally locked at the dimer interface.
source: Remarkably, the C-lobe of molecule B is conformationally locked at the dimer interface, where it buttresses the N-terminal part of the pointer helix of molecule A (Figures 1C and 2A,B).
evidence: The text explicitly describes the locked conformation with reference to figures.

claim: C-lobe mobility is required for HECT E3 activity.
source: C-lobe mobility, however, as enabled by a flexible linker between the N- and C-lobes of the HECT domain (Figure 1A), is required for HECT E3 activity (Verdecia et al., 2003).
evidence: The text cites previous literature establishing this requirement.

claim: The conformation of molecule B in the crystal reflects an auto-inhibited state.
source: We thus predict that the conformation of molecule B in the crystal reflects an auto-inhibited state.
evidence: The authors explicitly state their prediction based on the structural observations.

claim: The dimer interface buries a region of the C-lobe including Leu 4335, Met 4359, and Leu 4362.
source: This interpretation is underscored by the fact that the dimer interface buries a particular region of the C-lobe, including Leu 4335, Met 4359, and Leu 4362 (Figure 2A).
evidence: The text identifies specific residues buried at the interface with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: The homologous region in NEDD4-type E3 enzymes has been shown to interact with ubiquitin, facilitating the transfer of ubiquitin from E2 to E3.
source: The homologous region in NEDD4-type E3 enzymes has been shown to interact with ubiquitin, thereby facilitating the transfer of ubiquitin from the E2 to the E3 (Maspero et al., 2013; Kamadurai et al., 2009, 2013) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The text cites previous studies demonstrating this interaction.

claim: If HUWE1 oriented ubiquitin in a similar manner to NEDD4-type enzymes, this complex would clash with the HUWE1 dimer.
source: If HUWE1 oriented ubiquitin in a similar manner, this complex would clash with the HUWE1 dimer (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The text describes a structural incompatibility with reference to a figure.

claim: Truncation of the C-lobe by four residues or mutation of −4 Phe inhibits the auto-ubiquitination activities of various HECT E3 enzymes, including the HECT domain of HUWE1.
source: Consistently, truncation of the C-lobe by four residues or mutation of −4 Phe was found to inhibit the auto-ubiquitination acitivities of various HECT E3 enzymes, including the HECT domain of HUWE1 (Verdecia et al., 2003; Maspero et al., 2013; Kamadurai et al., 2013; Pandya et al., 2010; Salvat et al., 2004; Mari et al., 2014).
evidence: The text cites multiple studies demonstrating this effect.

claim: The C-tail of molecule B is fully resolved in the crystal structure.
source: Our crystal structure of HUWE1 has the C-tail of molecule B fully resolved (Figure 2C).
evidence: The text explicitly states this observation with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: −4 Phe is buried at the dimer interface, where it interacts with Phe 3955, Phe 3958, and the aliphatic side chain portion of Lys 3954 of molecule A in trans, and with Leu 4335 and Leu 4362 of the C-lobe in cis.
source: −4 Phe is buried at the dimer interface, where it interacts with Phe 3955, Phe 3958, and the aliphatic side chain portion of Lys 3954 of molecule A in trans, and with Leu 4335 and Leu 4362 of the C-lobe in cis (Figure 2D).
evidence: The text describes specific interactions with reference to Figure 2D.

claim: The tight engagement of −4 Phe at the dimer interface is incompatible with the C-tail reaching out to the N-lobe, as seen in an active conformation of the NEDD4-type E3 RSP5.
source: This tight engagement of −4 Phe at the dimer interface is incompatible with the C-tail reaching out to the N-lobe, as seen in an active conformation of the NEDD4-type E3 RSP5 (Kamadurai et al., 2013).
evidence: The text draws a comparison to a known active conformation from the literature.

claim: The conformation of molecule B in the crystal structure of HUWE1 represents an auto-inhibited state.
source: Taken together, we conclude that the conformation of molecule B in our crystal structure of HUWE1 represents an auto-inhibited state.
evidence: The authors explicitly state their conclusion based on multiple structural observations.

claim: The C-lobe of molecule A does not contact the dimer interface.
source: In contrast to the locked C-lobe conformation of molecule B, the C-lobe of molecule A does not contact the dimer interface (Figure 2A) and its C-tail could not be modeled (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The text explicitly states this observation with reference to figures.

claim: The C-tail of molecule A could not be modeled.
source: In contrast to the locked C-lobe conformation of molecule B, the C-lobe of molecule A does not contact the dimer interface (Figure 2A) and its C-tail could not be modeled (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The text explicitly states this limitation with reference to a figure.

claim: The C-lobe of molecule A forms peripheral, predominantly electrostatic lattice contacts with three neighboring molecules in the crystal.
source: Instead, the C-lobe of molecule A forms peripheral, predominantly electrostatic lattice contacts with three neighboring molecules in the crystal (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The text describes the lattice contacts with reference to a figure.

claim: The lattice interfaces and putative higher order oligomeric assemblies are not relevant in solution.
source: Neither of these interfaces or putative higher order oligomeric assemblies are relevant in solution (see below, Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion with reference to later figures.

claim: It is structurally conceivable that the C-lobe of molecule A is flexible in the context of the dimer and occupies catalytically relevant positions in solution.
source: In principle, it is conceivable structurally that the C-lobe of molecule A is flexible in the context of the dimer and that it occupies catalytically relevant positions, as observed in other HECT E3 enzymes, in solution (Figure 2—figure supplement 4)
evidence: The authors present a hypothesis based on structural considerations and comparison to other enzymes.

claim: HUWE1 (3951-4374) dimerizes in solution.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that HUWE1 (3951–4374) dimerizes in solution.
evidence: The authors explicitly state this conclusion based on SEC-MALS and SAXS data.

claim: At the lowest concentration tested (3 μM), the MALS-derived molecular weight of HUWE1 (3951-4374) is 54 kDa, very close to the MW of a monomer (53 kDa).
source: At the lowest concentration tested, the MALS-derived molecular weight (MW) of 54 kDa is very close to the MW of a monomer (53 kDa).
evidence: The text provides quantitative MALS data.

claim: With increasing protein concentration, the conformational equilibrium of HUWE1 (3951-4374) shifts toward a dimer.
source: With increasing protein concentration the conformational equilibrium shifts toward a dimer.
evidence: The text describes the concentration-dependent behavior observed in SEC-MALS experiments.

claim: At the highest concentration tested (378 μM), the MALS-derived MW of HUWE1 (3951-4374) is 93 kDa, consistent with a dominant population of the dimeric state.
source: At the highest concentration tested, the MALS analysis yields a MW of 93 kDa, in line with a dominant population of the dimeric state.
evidence: The text provides quantitative MALS data and interprets it.

claim: Simulated scattering profiles based on the crystal structure of the HUWE1 dimer approximate the experimental SAXS data well with a fit score χ of 1.4.
source: Indeed, simulated scattering profiles based on the crystal structure of the HUWE1 dimer approximate the experimental data well (Figure 3B), as reflected by an excellent fit score, χ, of 1.4 for a single model (average fit score for the single best models of three replicate runs: χ = 1.4 ± 0.1).
evidence: The text provides quantitative SAXS analysis results with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: Simulations based on the structures of either of the monomers seen in the crystal are unable to reproduce the experimental SAXS data well, with χ-values of 19.9 and 17.7 for molecules A and B, respectively.
source: In contrast, simulations based on the structures of either of the monomers seen in the crystal are unable to reproduce the experimental data well, with χ−values worsening to 19.9 and 17.7 for molecules A and B, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; average fit scores for the single best models of three replicate runs: χ = 20.3 ± 0.1 and 17.6 ± 0.2, respectively).
evidence: The text provides quantitative SAXS analysis results with reference to a figure.

claim: The SAXS data are inconsistent with a monomeric state of HUWE1 (3951-4374) but are in agreement with the structure of the crystallographic dimer.
source: The SAXS data are, therefore, inconsistent with a monomeric state of HUWE1 (3951–4374), but they are in agreement with the structure of the crystallographic dimer.
evidence: The authors explicitly state their interpretation of the SAXS data.

claim: The SAXS-derived radius of gyration (Rg) of HUWE1 (3951-4374) is 36 Å, significantly larger than the value expected for a monomer (25 Å) and consistent with the value calculated for the crystallographic dimer (35 Å).
source: In line with these analyses, the SAXS-derived radius of gyration (Rg), a measure of the molecular mass distribution, of HUWE1 (3951–4374) is significantly larger than the value expected for a monomer (experimental Rg = 36 Å; calculated Rg = 25 Å) and is, instead, consistent with the value calculated for the crystallographic dimer (Rg = 35 Å).
evidence: The text provides quantitative SAXS-derived Rg values and compares them to calculated values.

claim: The dimerization of HUWE1 in solution is not induced by the expression tag.
source: We can, therefore, conclude that the dimerization of HUWE1 in solution is not induced by the expression tag.
evidence: The authors explicitly state this conclusion based on SEC-MALS experiments comparing tagged and untagged protein.

claim: Untagged HUWE1 (3951-4374) dimerizes with a dissociation constant (KD) of approximately 3 μM.
source: Importantly, we also demonstrate that untagged HUWE1 (3951–4374) dimerizes using analytical ultracentrifugation (Figure 3C). The corresponding dissociation constant, KD, of ~3 μM, indicates that the dimerization of this construct is relatively weak in vitro, consistent with our SEC-MALS analyses.
evidence: The text provides quantitative AUC data with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: The dimerization of HUWE1 (3951-4374) is relatively weak in vitro.
source: The corresponding dissociation constant, KD, of ~3 μM, indicates that the dimerization of this construct is relatively weak in vitro, consistent with our SEC-MALS analyses.
evidence: The authors interpret the KD value to characterize the strength of dimerization.

claim: HUWE1 (3975-4374), which lacks the pointer helix, no longer dimerizes in SEC-MALS experiments, even at high concentrations of 380 μM.
source: Since the pointer helix is an integral part of the dimer interface, we expected the truncated construct to be monomeric. Indeed, this construct no longer dimerizes in SEC-MALS experiments, even at high concentrations of 380 μM, and its elution volume approaches that of the monomeric HECT domain (Figure 4A).
evidence: The text describes the experimental result with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: The MALS-derived MW of HUWE1 (3975-4374) is 51 kDa, close to the calculated MW of 50 kDa.
source: The MALS-derived MWs of 51 and 44 kDa for HUWE1 (3975–4374) and for the HECT domain are close to the calculated MWs of 50 and 47 kDa, respectively.
evidence: The text provides quantitative MALS data.

claim: The experimental SAXS profile of HUWE1 (3975-4374) is approximated well by a simulated profile based on the monomeric structure with a fit score χ of 1.3.
source: In line with these observations, the experimental SAXS profile of HUWE1 (3975–4374) is approximated well by a simulated profile based on the monomeric structure of this fragment, as extracted from our crystal structure (single best fit score: χ = 1.3; average fit score for the single best models of three replicate runs: χ = 1.30 ± 0.05) (Figure 4B).
evidence: The text provides quantitative SAXS analysis results with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: The SAXS-derived Rg-value of HUWE1 (3975-4374) is 27 Å, consistent with the calculated value for a monomer (26 Å).
source: The corresponding SAXS-derived Rg-value (27 Å) is also consistent with the calculated value for a monomer (26 Å).
evidence: The text provides quantitative SAXS-derived Rg values and compares them to calculated values.

claim: Ile 3969 of molecule A is at the core of the dimer interface, where it packs tightly against Leu 3966, Phe 3982, Val 3984, and Leu 3985 of subunit B.
source: Both residues form key hydrophobic contacts at the dimer interface: Ile 3969 of molecule A is at the core of the dimer interface, where it packs tightly against Leu 3966, Phe 3982, Val 3984, and Leu 3985 of subunit B (Figure 4C).
evidence: The text describes specific interactions with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: The I3969A and F3982A single mutant variants of HUWE1 (3951-4374) have MALS-derived MWs of 63 and 64 kDa, respectively, significantly lower than the WT (79 kDa), indicating that the conformational equilibria of these variants are shifted toward the monomeric state.
source: Both proteins elute at larger volumes than the WT. The MALS-derived MWs of 63 and 64 kDa for the I3969A and F3982A variants, respectively, are significantly lower than the MW derived for the WT (79 kDa), indicating that the conformational equilibria of these variants are shifted toward the monomeric state.
evidence: The text provides quantitative MALS data and interprets the results.

claim: The I3969A/F3982A double mutant variant of HUWE1 (3951-4374) has a MALS-derived MW of 53 kDa, close to the calculated monomeric weight (50 kDa), demonstrating that this protein variant does not dimerize significantly.
source: The simultaneous mutation of both sites, I3969A/F3982A, results in an additional increase in the SEC-elution volume (Figure 4F). The corresponding MALS-derived MW of 53 kDa is now close the calculated monomeric weight (50 kDa), which demonstrates that this protein variant does not dimerize significantly any more.
evidence: The text provides quantitative MALS data and interprets the results with reference to Figure 4F.

claim: His 3962 is among a subset of residues in the dimerization region that were found to be mutated in human tumors.
source: Notably, one of the mutation sites that we selected for our studies, Ile 3969, is among a subset of residues in the dimerization region that were found to be mutated in human tumors (cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma: I3969N and I3969V [Pickering et al., 2014]).
evidence: The text cites a study identifying tumor-associated mutations.

claim: The H3962D variant of HUWE1 (3951-4374) has a MALS-derived MW of 62 kDa, confirming that the dimerization capacity of this variant is reduced significantly.
source: Indeed, SEC-MALS experiments show that this variant elutes at larger volumes than the WT (Figure 4G), and the MALS-derived MW of 62 kDa confirms that the dimerization capacity of this variant is reduced significantly.
evidence: The text provides quantitative MALS data and interprets the results with reference to Figure 4G.

claim: HUWE1 self-associates in cells.
source: Strikingly, we find that HUWE1 self-associates (Figure 5A).
evidence: The text describes the result of co-IP experiments with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: The F3982A and I3969A variants of HUWE1 both show a marked reduction in their abilities to associate with WT HUWE1 in cells.
source: In contrast to WT HUWE1, the F3982A and I3969A variants both show a marked reduction in their abilities to associate with WT HUWE1, analogous to the disruptive effect of these mutations on HUWE1 dimerization that was observed in vitro (Figure 5A).
evidence: The text describes the result of co-IP experiments with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: HUWE1 dimerizes in vitro and self-associates in cells through the same key contacts that mediate the formation of the crystallographic dimer.
source: Taken together, these studies confirm that HUWE1 dimerizes in vitro and self-associates in cells and that both processes depend on the same key contacts that mediate the formation of the crystallographic dimer.
evidence: The authors explicitly state this conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: All dimerization-deficient mutated variants (I3969A, F3982A, I3969A/F3982A, and H3962D) are more active than the WT in auto-ubiquitination assays in vitro.
source: We find that all of the mutated variants are, indeed, more active than the WT.
evidence: The text describes the results of in vitro activity assays.

claim: The stimulatory effect on auto-ubiquitination activity is most pronounced for the double mutant variant I3969A/F3982A, consistent with the dimer being most destabilized for this variant.
source: The stimulatory effect is most pronounced for the double mutant variant, I3969A/F3982A, consistent with the dimer being most destabilized for this variant.
evidence: The text describes the results of in vitro activity assays and interprets them.

claim: The activity of HUWE1 WT decreases slightly with increasing protein concentrations, which can be explained by concentration-dependent changes in the population of the dimeric state.
source: The activity of HUWE1 WT decreases slightly with increasing protein concentrations, which can be explained, at least qualitatively, by concentration-dependent changes in the population of the dimeric state.
evidence: The text describes the observation and provides an interpretation.

claim: MCL1 is ubiquitinated significantly more strongly by the truncated, dimerization-deficient constructs of HUWE1 (3975-4374 and 3993-4374) than by HUWE1 (3951-4374) that dimerizes.
source: In line with our model, we find that MCL1 is ubiquitinated significantly more strongly by the truncated, dimerization-deficient constructs of HUWE1 than by HUWE1 (3951–4374) that dimerizes.
evidence: The text describes the results of in vitro substrate ubiquitination assays.

claim: Both MCL1 and C-MYC are ubiquitinated more strongly upon expression of the dimerization-deficient HUWE1 variants I3969A and F3982A than in the presence of the WT enzyme in cells.
source: Interestingly, our studies show that both MCL1 and C-MYC are, indeed, ubiquitinated more strongly upon expression of the dimerization-deficient HUWE1 variants I3969A and F3982A than in the presence of the WT enzyme (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: The text describes the results of cell-based activity assays with reference to Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: The stimulatory effect toward MCL1 and C-MYC is significantly more pronounced for the F3982A variant than for the I3969A variant.
source: It should be noted, however, that the stimulatory effect toward either substrate is significantly more pronounced for the F3982A than for the I3969A variant.
evidence: The text describes the observation from cell-based activity assays.

claim: HUWE1 exists in an, at least partially, inhibited state in HeLa cells.
source: Evidently, HUWE1 exists in an, at least partially, inhibited state in HeLa cells.
evidence: The authors draw this conclusion from the observation that the catalytically dead variant shows similar low background ubiquitination as the WT.

claim: A disruption of the dimer interface of HUWE1 releases inhibitory restraints on its catalytic activity, both in vitro and in cells.
source: Taken together, these studies demonstrate that a disruption of the dimer interface of HUWE1 releases inhibitory restraints on its catalytic activity, both in vitro and in cells.
evidence: The authors explicitly state this conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: HUWE1 constructs containing the activation segment (3759-4374, 3810-4374, and 3843-4374) bind to the p14ARF-peptide with dissociation constants in the low micromolar range (7.7, 6, and 5.2 μM, respectively).
source: Interestingly, we find that all HUWE1 constructs that contain the activation segment, that is, HUWE1 (3759–4374), HUWE1 (3810–4374), and HUWE1 (3843–4374), bind to the p14ARF-peptide with dissociation constants in the low micromolar range (7.7, 6, and 5.2 μM, respectively).
evidence: The text provides quantitative fluorescence polarization data.

claim: Shorter constructs of HUWE1 that lack the activation segment display significantly weaker affinities for p14ARF, with dissociation constants ranging from 230 to 340 μM.
source: In contrast, shorter constructs of HUWE1 that are lacking the activation segment display significantly weaker affinities for p14ARF, with dissociation constants ranging from 230 to 340 μM.
evidence: The text provides quantitative fluorescence polarization data.

claim: A major binding site for p14ARF on HUWE1 resides in the activation segment.
source: This implies that a major binding site for p14ARF on HUWE1 resides in the activation segment.
evidence: The authors draw this conclusion from fluorescence polarization experiments with the isolated activation segment.

claim: The activities of HUWE1 (3843-4374), (3896-4374), and (3951-4374) are all significantly inhibited by the p14ARF-peptide in auto-ubiquitination assays.
source: Surprisingly, we find that the activities of HUWE1 (3843–4374), (3896–4374), and (3951–4374), are all significantly inhibited by the p14ARF-peptide.
evidence: The text describes the results of in vitro activity assays.

claim: For the isolated HECT domain, no clear p14ARF-mediated inhibitory effect is observed.
source: For the isolated HECT domain, no clear p14ARF-mediated inhibitory effect is observed.
evidence: The text describes the results of in vitro activity assays.

claim: The p14ARF-derived peptide can inhibit the auto-ubiquitination activity of HUWE1 in a manner that is independent of the activation segment.
source: Our studies thus show that the p14ARF-derived peptide - while interacting most strongly with the activation segment of HUWE1 - can, in principle, inhibit the auto-ubiquitination activity of HUWE1 in a manner that is independent of the activation segment.
evidence: The authors draw this conclusion from the observation that constructs lacking the activation segment can still be inhibited by p14ARF.

claim: The p14ARF-derived peptide triggers a marked shift in the SEC profile of HUWE1 (3843-4374), indicative of oligomerization.
source: Strikingly, the peptide triggers a marked shift in the SEC profile of HUWE1 (3843–4374), indicative of oligomerization.
evidence: The text describes the results of SEC experiments.

claim: Shorter constructs of HUWE1 that lack the activation segment (3896-4374, 3951-4374, and 3993-4374) are not affected by the presence of the p14ARF peptide in SEC experiments.
source: Shorter constructs of HUWE1 that lack the activation segment (HUWE1 [3896–4374], HUWE1 [3951–4374], and HUWE1 [3993–4374]) are not affected by the presence of the peptide, in line with the results of the fluorescence polarization studies (Figure 10C–E).
evidence: The text describes the results of SEC experiments with reference to Figures 10C-E.

claim: p14ARF may shift the conformational equilibrium of HUWE1 toward the inhibited dimeric state by capturing the activating segment.
source: Taken together, these experiments are consistent with the intriguing notion that p14ARF may shift the conformational equilibrium of HUWE1 toward the inhibited dimeric state by capturing the activating segment.
evidence: The authors explicitly state this hypothesis based on their experimental observations.

claim: An additional/alternate mode of p14ARF-mediated inhibition of HUWE1 is independent of the activation segment.
source: An additional/alternate mode of p14ARF-mediated inhibition of HUWE1 is independent of the activation segment.
evidence: The authors explicitly state this conclusion based on their experimental observations.

claim: HUWE1 is overexpressed in many tumors.
source: HUWE1 is overexpressed in many tumors (Confalonieri et al., 2009; Adhikary et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2005; Yoon et al., 2005; Myant et al., 2016) and has been studied intensively in this context.
evidence: The text cites multiple studies documenting HUWE1 overexpression in tumors.

claim: Both pro-oncogenic and tumor-suppressor functions of HUWE1 have been documented in different tumor models.
source: Surprisingly, both pro-oncogenic and tumor-suppressor functions of HUWE1 have been documented in different tumor models.
evidence: The text states this observation about HUWE1's dual roles.

claim: HUWE1 can target oncoproteins such as N-MYC, C-MYC, and MCL1 for degradation.
source: HUWE1 can target oncoproteins, such as N-MYC, C-MYC (Myant et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2008; Inoue et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2009), and MCL1 (Myant et al., 2016; Zhong et al., 2005; Warr et al., 2005), but also the tumor suppressor protein p53 (Chen et al., 2005) and the co-factor of MYC, MIZ1 (Inoue et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2010; Peter et al., 2014) for degradation.
evidence: The text cites multiple studies documenting HUWE1 substrates.

claim: HUWE1 associates with and is inhibited by the tumor suppressor p14ARF.
source: HUWE1 associates with and is inhibited by the tumor suppressor p14ARF ('Alternative Reading Frame' in the CDKN2A gene) (Chen et al., 2005), a key activator of p53-mediated cell cycle arrest and apoptosis (Ozenne et al., 2010).
evidence: The text cites a study documenting this interaction and inhibition.

claim: p14ARF is best known for its ability to inhibit the HDM2 ubiquitin ligase that targets p53 for degradation.
source: p14ARF is best known for its ability to inhibit the HDM2 ubiquitin ligase that targets p53 for degradation (Sherr, 2001).
evidence: The text cites a study documenting this well-known function of p14ARF.

claim: p19ARF inhibits proliferation of p53- and Mdm2-deficient mouse embryo fibroblasts, demonstrating that ARF has growth-suppressive functions independent of both p53 and MDM2.
source: However, p19ARF, the mouse orthologue of human p14ARF, inhibits proliferation of p53- and Mdm2-deficient mouse embryo fibroblasts, formally demonstrating that ARF has growth-suppressive functions that are independent of both p53 and MDM2 (Weber et al., 2000).
evidence: The text cites a study demonstrating p53-independent functions of ARF.

claim: The regulation of HUWE1 activity by p14ARF is implicated in both the p53-dependent and p53-independent functions of p14ARF.
source: The regulation of HUWE1 activity by p14ARF is implicated in both the p53-dependent and p53-independent functions of p14ARF (Chen et al., 2005).
evidence: The text cites a study implicating HUWE1 regulation in p14ARF functions.

claim: HUWE1 belongs to the HECT family of ubiquitin ligases.
source: HUWE1 belongs to the HECT (Homologous to E6AP C-Terminus)-family of ubiquitin ligases (E3 enzymes) (Huibregtse et al., 1995).
evidence: The text cites the study that defined the HECT family.

claim: HECT ligases are characterized by a conserved C-terminal catalytic domain, the 'HECT domain', that transfers ubiquitin molecules from ubiquitin-loaded E2 enzymes onto substrate proteins.
source: These enzymes are characterized by a conserved C-terminal catalytic domain, the 'HECT domain', that serves to transfer ubiquitin molecules from ubiquitin-loaded E2 enzymes onto substrate proteins (Huang et al., 1999).
evidence: The text cites a study describing the function of the HECT domain.

claim: The HECT domain consists of two lobes, a smaller C-terminal 'C'-lobe and a larger 'N'-lobe that are connected by a flexible linker.
source: The HECT domain consists of two lobes, a smaller C-terminal 'C'-lobe and a larger 'N'-lobe that are connected by a flexible linker (Huang et al., 1999; Verdecia et al., 2003).
evidence: The text cites studies describing the structure of the HECT domain.

claim: The N-lobe of HECT domains associates with E2 enzymes.
source: The N-lobe associates with E2 enzymes (Huang et al., 1999) and, at least in the NEDD4-subfamily, with a ubiquitin molecule of regulatory function (Maspero et al., 2011, 2013; Ogunjimi et al., 2010; French et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: The text cites studies describing N-lobe functions.

claim: The C-lobe of HECT domains harbors the catalytic cysteine and interacts with the ubiquitin molecule that ought to be transferred to the substrate.
source: In contrast, the C-lobe harbors the catalytic cysteine and interacts with the ubiquitin molecule that ought to be transferred to the substrate (Maspero et al., 2013; Kamadurai et al., 2009, 2013; Kim and Huibregtse, 2009).
evidence: The text cites studies describing C-lobe functions.

claim: HUWE1 is a large protein of 482 kDa that is mostly uncharacterized structurally, with the exception of the C-terminal HECT domain, a UBA domain, a BH3 domain, and a UBM1 domain.
source: HUWE1 is a large protein of 482 kDa that is mostly uncharacterized structurally, with the exception of the C-terminal HECT domain (defined here as residues 3993–4374; PDB IDs: 3H1D (Pandya et al., 2010) and 3G1N), a ubiquitin-associated (UBA) domain (residues 1316–1355, PDB ID: 2EKK), a BH3 domain (residues 1976–1990, PDB ID: 5C6H) that interacts with MCL1 (Zhong et al., 2005; Warr et al., 2005), and a UBM1 domain of unknown function (residues 2951–3003, PDB ID: 2MUL).
evidence: The text describes the known structural elements of HUWE1 with citations.

claim: The dimerization region and the activation segment of HUWE1 are disproportionately highly conserved across the family of HUWE1 orthologues, including lower eukaryotic ones.
source: In line with the important functions of the dimerization region and the activation segment in controlling the conformational equilibrium of HUWE1, both regions are disproportionately highly conserved across the family of HUWE1 orthologues, including lower eukaryotic ones (Figure 11).
evidence: The text describes the conservation pattern with reference to Figure 11.

claim: The activation segment of HUWE1 may serve as an intramolecular 'wedge' that disrupts the HUWE1 dimer when the ligase ought to be active.
source: We imagine that the activation segment serves as an intramolecular 'wedge' that disrupts the HUWE1 dimer when the ligase ought to be active.
evidence: The authors present a model based on their structural and functional observations.

claim: The conformational equilibrium and activity of HUWE1 is modulated by yet uncharacterized domain interactions in the context of full-length HUWE1 and by macromolecular factors.
source: We propose that the conformational equilibrium and, hence, the activity of HUWE1 is modulated by yet uncharacterized domain interactions in the context of full-length HUWE1 and by macromolecular factors that will determine not only the local concentrations of HUWE1 in the cell, but also the accessibility of the dimerization region and the activation segment for their intramolecular engagement (Figure 12).
evidence: The authors propose a model with reference to Figure 12.

claim: A binding site for PCNA ('PIP-box') has been mapped to residues 3880-3887 of HUWE1, coinciding with the activation segment.
source: Interestingly, a binding site for PCNA ('PIP-box') has recently been mapped to residues 3880‐3887 of HUWE1 (Choe et al., 2016), thus coinciding with the activation segment.
evidence: The text cites a recent study identifying a PCNA binding site.

claim: Several point mutations identified in human tumors fall into the dimerization region and result in non-conservative amino acid changes of interfacing residues.
source: For instance, several point mutations that were identified in human tumors fall into the dimerization region and result in non-conservative amino acid changes of interfacing residues.
evidence: The text describes tumor-associated mutations in the dimerization region.

claim: His 3962 and Ile 3969 are critical for dimerization and for the auto-inhibition of HUWE1.
source: We show that two of these sites, His 3962 and Ile 3969, are critical for dimerization and for the auto-inhibition of HUWE1.
evidence: The authors explicitly state this conclusion based on their mutagenesis and activity studies.

claim: There may be selective pressure in some human tumors to enhance the activity of HUWE1 and to render it resistant to inhibition by p14ARF.
source: These observations are in line with the notion that there may be selective pressure, at least in some human tumors, to enhance the activity of HUWE1 and to render it resistant to inhibition by p14ARF.
evidence: The authors present an interpretation of the tumor mutation data.
